items.title: Jimmy Cobb — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: It turns out I go on the road with Earl Bostic.

ctx.x: Yeah. Carmen Leggio, Keter Betts, and I forget what the drummer’s name was. He was a great drummer. He was a good drummer. I used to admire him, because he had a fast foot and he could play real good. I wish I could think of his name. I wish I could find him, because I’d like to remember him or even to know if he’s still alive. I met Keter. We got to be friends. They would go and come back. One time he went and came back, he was with Earl Bostic. He told me, he says, “Look. Our drummer’s quitting. Do you want to…
That’s the one that faces to the back?

items.title: Walter Booker and Jimmy Cobb interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995
items.q: Keter Betts got me a job with Earl Bostic’s band and I left town.

ctx.x: Tell us one of the gigs that you were on when you in your own mind said I’ve arrived — I’m a player, I’m on the scene and I have a voice here.

Well I think that must have been when Keter Betts got me a job with Earl Bostic’s band and I left town. I didn’t say I’ve arrived, I say I’m leaving. Which is, so I left, from my standpoint, I’m leaving. But you know that was a pretty good thing because I didn’t know if I was ever going to get out of the town. I got to be 21 years old and I got to leave so it was great. I went to New York and then from New York I stayed in New York, which

that was my passage out of Washington. Not that I didn’t love Washington, I still love it. But it’s not like you’re going to make a living around there playing music. Maybe some people do but I didn’t think I could. I figured New York was the place for me. And it turned out. It worked out.
